opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is to separate decisions that are reversible from ones that aren't. Most day-to-day technical choices you can undo, so you should move fast and let the team experiment. But a small number of decisions really define what the company becomes: what kind of model you bet on, how you allocate compute, whether you focus on long context or reasoning or agents first. Those you can't easily walk back, because they shape your data pipeline, your infrastructure, your hiring, even your culture.

For those big decisions, I try to reason from first principles rather than from what competitors are doing. In AI it's very tempting to look at what the leading labs released last month and follow. But by the time you've copied it, the frontier has moved. So the question I ask is: what do we believe is fundamentally true about how intelligence scales, and where is the bottleneck going to be one or two years from now? If you get that right, the specific product choices follow.

I also think technical decisions and organizational decisions are the same thing. If you decide that, say, reinforcement learning is going to be core to your next generation of models, that isn't just a research direction. It means you need different people, different evaluation systems, different ways of measuring progress. A lot of companies make the technical call but don't change the organization, and then the decision never really gets executed.

And finally, you have to accept that you'll be wrong sometimes. The goal isn't to be right every time. It's to have a good process: be clear about your assumptions, watch for signals that they're breaking, and be willing to change course quickly when the evidence says so. In a field moving this fast, the ability to correct yourself is probably more valuable than being right the first time.

r001.rationale: The response says a small number of technical decisions can shape what a company becomes, but gives no estimate that they determine at least 50–60% of its direction.

r002.rationale: It mentions letting the team experiment and watching for evidence that assumptions are breaking, but does not state that good technical decisions require evidence from many experiments.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that most of the important technical decisions are really bets on where the field is going, not just judgments about what works today. And the hard part is that you have to make them with incomplete information, and the cost of being wrong compounds.

When I think about it, there are a few things I keep coming back to.

The first is to try to reason from first principles rather than from what everyone else is doing. In this field, a lot of people are watching the same papers and the same demos, so if you just follow the consensus you end up building the same thing as everyone else, a little bit later. The question I try to ask is: what does the scaling law actually say, what does the data say, what is physically and mathematically true about this problem? And then, given that, where will things be in two or three years, not where are they now?

The second is that a technical decision at a company is never purely technical. It determines what kind of people you hire, how you allocate compute, what you say no to. So when we decide, for example, to prioritize long context, or to focus on a particular kind of model rather than spreading across many, that is really a decision about the identity of the company. You have to be willing to give things up. If you try to hedge on everything, you have no edge on anything.

The third thing is about time horizon. There is a constant tension between what will make the product better next quarter and what will put you in the right position in three years. My bias is toward the longer horizon, because in AI the technology moves so fast that optimizing too hard for the current generation usually means you are building on a foundation that is about to disappear. But you also cannot ignore the present completely, because the present is what pays for the future and gives you the feedback signals to know whether your bets are right.

And then, honestly, the last part is accepting uncertainty. I don't think anyone can be right about everything. What you can do is make decisions that are reversible when they can be, be very deliberate about the ones that are not, and set up the organization so that you learn quickly when you are wrong. The teams that win are not necessarily the ones with the best initial guess. They are the ones that update the fastest.

r002.rationale: The response refers to reasoning from scaling laws and data and learning quickly, but it does not state that good technical decisions require evidence from many experiments.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is to ask what you believe will matter in the long term. A technical decision can look attractive because it improves a benchmark today, but if it doesn’t help you build toward that longer-term goal, it may not be the right decision for the company.

Then you have to turn that belief into something you can test. What is the key assumption? What experiment would change your mind? I like to distinguish between having conviction about the direction and being flexible about the approach. You need enough conviction to invest in something difficult, but you also need to respond when the evidence tells you that your approach isn’t working.

And these decisions are also organizational decisions. When you choose a technical direction, you’re choosing what talent to hire, where to spend compute, and what your team will learn over the next year. So I would evaluate not only the immediate result, but also whether the work makes us better equipped to solve the next problem.

r002.rationale: It recommends testing key assumptions with an experiment and responding to evidence, but does not state that good decisions require evidence from many experiments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to be clear about what you believe and where you’re uncertain. A technical decision can shape the company for years, but you’re always making it with incomplete information.

So I try to separate the long-term direction from the assumptions we can test today. What capability do we think will matter? What experiment would give us evidence that we’re moving toward it? And what result would make us change our minds?

You also have to consider the team. Choosing a technical direction means deciding where people spend their time, what kind of expertise you build, and what you’re willing to give up. You can’t pursue every promising idea equally.

For me, the goal is to have conviction about the problem, while staying flexible about the solution. Make a clear choice, learn as quickly as possible, and don’t let the fact that it was your decision become a reason to defend it.
